Sorry, but my own, admittedly anecdotal, experience with Steam early access titles suggests that most of them are ill-considered, at best, or scams, at worst. Further, I can't fathom the justification being used to allow their sale on a platform for which the primary selling point is guaranteed compatibility, when base functionality of an early release isn't guaranteed by definition. The whole concept boggles my mind.

Yeah, I'm not much for early access either. I don't even pre-order pretty much anything. I'll wait a week or two after stable release to give any gamebreaking issues time to surface and see if I'm still interested at that time. A week or two is not a long time to wait, and I get a lot out of it. But there's no denying that early access is now an entrenched part of the industry. Not ever game will do it, but oftentimes a "stable" release will be just as buggy as an early access title, so you're effectively playing the game while it's still in development whether it's called "early access" or not. The only way I can think of to combat this trend is to simply not buy games until I feel they're ready, and that means waiting on the "not quite done" stable releases that we've been seeing lately.

That's pretty much what I've been doing. I think the last release title I bought was Grey Goo, because I fell for all that "We are Westwood!" crap Petroglyph was spouting -- I even convinced several friends to buy into it -- and we all know what a disappointment that game turned out to be. I'm sticking to GOTY sales now, with the occasional exception made for Steam's seasonal sales.

I've thought about joining the console peasant army, though, which is why this is interesting to me. I just can't imagine M$ letting this fly. I mean... I can... they clearly want a piece of the pie... but damn, consoles used to mean something.

The weird thing to me is that consoles are losing the last things that keep them distinct from PCs. Splitscren support and local multiplayer is going away, and physical media is too. Nowadays even if you buy an Xbox One game on disc, there's a good chance you'll have to download up to 10Gb of data to make it playable. And with early access titles now making their way to consoles, plenty of games are dropping support for physical media entirely. I'm afraid that before long consoles will be nothing more than a "PC-lite" that's nothing more than the PC experience with older hardware.

The death and rebirth of FMV ["Full Motion Video"] in games

This is kind of an interesting topic. I remember early FMV games that came out to coincide with the rise in popularity of CD-ROM drives. A CD had way more storage space than a 3.5" floppy and even most consumer-level hard drives which made it a great candidate for the comparatively large video and audio requirements of FMV. It wound up being little more than a fad, however, because of poor implementation and the fact that FMV was only a side-show...the actual game still had the usual hurdles to jump through to be compelling and successful.

That's a good point. The only games I remember playing with FMV cut-scenes were the early Twisted Metal games. I don't think there's anything inherently wrong with FMV, but seeing them in Twisted Metal felt a little jarring because of how different it is from the gameplay visuals. I think that problem starts to go away because graphics are getting so much better; it's not as much of a transition when a game cuts to real video. But by the same token it might also mean FMV isn't necessary because computer generated cut scenes start to look realistic enough to cut in on whatever advantage FMV would provide.

Ya, the whole uncanny valley thing is tough to overcome. Talented developers will find a way to make it work now that the issues aren't about hardware anymore. I can't say I'd be too enthusiastic about a game that try to play up the FMV elements but I'd at least try to be open minded about on that has solid gameplay with FMV components adding to the experience.
